name: Woleaian
confidence_why: Mayer's 2025 reference grammar describes regular penultimate stress, cued by pitch, that moves with suffixation and that speakers insist on, while Sohn's 1975 reference grammar remarks in passing that all vowels are pronounced with equal intensity and gives no stress rule, a claim Mayer answers directly by showing that intensity is not the cue for Woleaian stress.

catalog_quote: Primary stress in Woleaian is regularly penultimate, meaning that it usually falls on the syllable preceding the syllable containing the devoiced vowel. ... The words that deviate from the regular penultimate stress pattern are those that end in a voiced vowel. In words that end in a word-final voiced vowel, stress is usually placed on this vowel, i.e., the final syllable, e.g., [fi.ˈta] /fita/ fita ‘(to) fish’. However, there are some words with a final voiced vowel where stress does fall on the penultimate syllable, as in [ˈsiː.ɾo] /siɾo/ silo ‘pig’. I could not find a predictive environment that determines on whether stress falls on the ultimate or penultimate syllable in case of a voiced final vowel in the data. ... All of this notwithstanding, I have found no instances in which stress is contrastive, i.e., different words that are only distinguished in their stress pattern, which is to be expected for a non-Phillippines Austronesian language (Himmelmann and Kaufman 2021, 372). ... These forms, and the handful of monolexemic forms with more than three syllables, additionally have secondary stress. Secondary stress is regularly placed on the first CV syllable of the phonological word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word, i.e. the syllable before the (utterance-finally devoiced) final vowel. The one systematic deviation is words whose final vowel is voiced (non-devoicible): these usually carry final stress (fita [fi.ˈta]), though a few such words (siilo 'pig', weri 'see', sari 'child') keep penultimate stress with no predictive environment found. Stress is never contrastive. The main phonetic correlate is higher pitch on the stressed syllable (Mayer says it could alternatively be called pitch accent); intonation contours override the stress-pitch difference; unstressed vowels reduce.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress is regularly placed on the first CV syllable of the phonological word' (p. 92), found in compounds, reduplicated forms, host+affix/clitic words and the few monolexemic words of more than three syllables, e.g. [ˌti.pəˈnœ.xu̥] tipeneogiu '(to be) aware', [ˌmʷa.ʃə.ŋa.ˈte.ti̥] mwashengateti 'seashore' (Table 2.27, p. 93).
new_statements.exceptions: Words ending in a voiced vowel: usually final stress; a handful (siilo 'pig', weri 'to see', sari 'child') have penultimate stress despite the voiced final vowel, so stress is 'partly lexically determined' for that small class (pp. 82-84, 92). Loanwords retain source-language stress/accent and can show aberrant patterns (§2.3.5, p. 92). Some prefixes/clitics (se- 'one') are always unstressed; the clitic ɾe=sa attracts secondary stress (p. 60-61). Sohn 1975 (p. 37) had claimed all vowels are pronounced with equal intensity and gave no word-stress rule; Mayer (p. 108) explicitly rejects that while agreeing stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word: nouns/verbs with their affixes and clitics, compounds and reduplications count as one phonological word, so stress moves rightward as enclitics are added (faliuwe [fæ.ˈɾʉ.w̥e] 'island' vs faliuwe we [fæ.ɾʉ.ˈwe.w̥e] 'the island' vs faliuwe kawe [fæ.ɾʉ.wə.ˈka.w̥e] 'the islands', p. 91). 'Penultimate' is counted including the utterance-finally devoiced final vowel. Word-level stress is distinguished from utterance-level intonation (§2.4.1, pp. 93-101). No quantitative acoustic study; based on the author's corpus and cursory Praat checks.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottocode wole1240 covers all six atoll varieties (Woleai, Eauripik, Ifaluk, Faraulap, Elato, Lamotrek); Mayer 2025 §1.5 (p. 27) says dialect differences are marginal and mainly in vowel realisation and intonation/prosody, and his description draws on speakers from the Outer Islands generally. Sohn 1975 (§0.4, p. 5) is explicitly limited to the Woleai-atoll dialect. No separate glottocodes exist for the atoll varieties as far as the Glottolog record shows.

readall_conflicts: The one work in scope (the OSF preregistration) is silent, so it neither confirms nor challenges the catalog. For the record, the two sources already held by the project from the earlier reading disagree with each other: Sohn 1975 (Woleaian Reference Grammar, p. 37; file) states 'In Woleaian, however, intensity is not particularly significant, because all vowels are pronounced with equal intensity in general', i.e. no word stress, whereas Mayer 2025 (A grammar of Woleaian, pp. 91-92, §2.4) states 'Primary stress in Woleaian is regularly penultimate' with final stress usually on a word-final voiced vowel and explicitly says (p. ~101, comparison with Sohn) 'I diverge from the analysis that "..all vowels are pronounced with equal intensity" (Sohn 1975, 37)' while agreeing that stress is not contrastive. The catalog follows Mayer 2025, the fuller and more recent phonetic analysis; the registration adds nothing to that verification.

sources.note: §2.4 Stress and Intonation, pp. 91-93 (pp. 91-93): primary stress regularly penultimate (the syllable before the devoiced final vowel); words ending in a voiced vowel usually take final stress (fita [fi.ˈta] 'fish'), with a few lexical exceptions (siilo [ˈsiː.ɾo] 'pig'); secondary stress on the first CV syllable of the phonological word; stress never contrastive; main correlate is pitch (could be called pitch accent), intonation overrides it; explicitly disagrees with Sohn 1975's 'equal intensity' claim (p. 108). Also p. 39 (typological profile) and pp. 82-84 (final voiced vowels).

sources.note: §1.9 Pitches and Intonation Contours, p. 37 (p. 51): 'In Woleaian, however, intensity is not particularly significant, because all vowels are pronounced with equal intensity in general.' No word-stress rule; describes four pitch levels (1-4) and three sentence-level intonation contours (2-4-2 yes/no questions; 3-3-1 wh-questions, commands, statements; 2-4-2-3-1 with internal pause), pp. 37-43. Chapter 1 has no other stress/accent mention.
